text:
Stop asking AI to “clean up” your meeting notes.

Give it a finish line:

“Turn these sample notes into a table with four columns: task, owner, deadline, and source sentence. If an owner or date is missing, write unknown. Don't fill the gaps.”

Then check the table against the notes.

1) Does every task point back to something someone actually said?
2) Did it turn a suggestion into a commitment?
3) Are the missing details still visible?

Use a made-up example first. For real work, use your organization's approved tools and data rules.

The useful part is the review step. A tidy action list can still be wrong.

Once the small example works, save the instructions and reuse them. You now have a workflow you can inspect instead of a vague request you have to rewrite.

Give your first agent a job with a clear stopping point.

Example: prepare a reading list from a folder of sample documents.

The input:
A small set of documents you've approved for the test.

The job:
Find items about one topic. Return the filename, a short summary, and the passage supporting it.

The stopping point:
A draft list for you to review. No sending, deleting, or changing the source files.

Test it with three documents, including one that doesn't belong. Check whether it leaves that one out and whether each summary matches its source.

Only then consider adding a scheduled run or more documents.

This is a build plan, not a claim that every agent tool supports the same features. Choose the tool after you've defined the job.

A small workflow you can check beats a sprawling assistant you can't explain.

Before buying another tool for missed inquiries, trace one inquiry through the business.

Where did it arrive?
Who was supposed to see it?
What counted as a response?
Where did the handoff stop?

If nobody owns the next step, an integration can move the message faster and still leave it unanswered.

Start with a simple process map. Name the person responsible, the expected response window, and what happens when they're unavailable.

Then test the smallest change on sample inquiries.

Track response time and whether each inquiry reaches the right person. Compare the same measures before and after. Don't turn a rough estimate into a savings claim.

This is the order I want Clockout to follow: Audit → Optimize → Automate.

The process has to be clear enough to know what the technology is supposed to improve.

I grew up in Roscoe, Illinois, and played Division I baseball at Northern Illinois University.

During college summers I worked for the Winnebago County Highway Department. Later came product and operations work at Uber, then digital product work at Walgreens.

Now I'm building Clockout as a solo founder.

Those are different environments. The thread I want to carry into this business is practical: understand the work, make the handoff clear, and build something people can actually use.

That's also how I want to teach AI.

Start with a task someone recognizes. Show the steps. Explain how to check the result. Give them enough understanding to try it themselves.

I don't need a dramatic origin story to explain that direction.

I want the work and the explanation to be useful.

“Can you sort this out?” is a rough starting point for an AI task.

Before pasting that work request into a chat, split it into four pieces:

The deliverable:
What should you have when the task is finished?

The material:
Which notes, files or examples should it use?

The limits:
What must it leave alone? What information is still missing?

The check:
How will you decide whether the result is usable?

Try it with a fictional request to organize a team update. Ask for a draft outline, not a polished report. See whether the outline contains the sections you actually need before asking for the full version.

For workplace material, follow your organization's tool and data rules.

A clearer task gives you something better to review. Save that task description when it works, and adjust it when the work changes.

A useful document-review agent starts with two versions of one document.

Here's a small build plan:

1) Choose a baseline file and a revised file. Give each a clear version label.

2) Have the agent return proposed changes in a table: old passage, new passage, location, and why the difference might matter.

3) Keep the original passages beside its explanation. You should be able to inspect the comparison without hunting through both files.

4) Add a deliberate trap to the test documents: move a paragraph without changing its wording. Does the agent report a new policy, or recognize that the text only moved?

5) Review the table yourself before accepting anything. Keep source documents read-only during this test.

Tool support varies. Check that your chosen tool can read both versions and point to the relevant passages before expanding the build.

Get the comparison right on a small sample before putting recurring document reviews on a schedule.

A follow-up reminder can fire on time and still be useless.

Suppose a job is waiting for a customer's missing document. The reminder says “follow up,” but the employee still has to find the job, work out what's missing, and check whether someone already asked.

That recurring search is part of the bottleneck.

Write down the minimum information the person needs:

- The job being held up
- The specific missing item
- The last contact and response
- Who takes the next action
- What closes the follow-up

Then decide where that information belongs and who keeps it current.

Test the revised handoff on sample jobs. Check whether someone can take the next step without reconstructing the history.

Automation becomes easier to evaluate once you know what a useful reminder must contain.

Faster notifications won't help much if every recipient has to investigate from scratch.

One part of my background worth keeping in the story: college-summer work for Winnebago County Highway Department.

It belongs alongside the product and operations work that came later. I don't want the AI part of my story to erase everything that came before it.

I'm building Clockout, and the direction I want is straightforward: get close enough to the work to understand the problem.

That also shapes what I want to share here.

If a task is confusing, show a clearer way to approach it. If a tool looks useful, explain the job it could do and how to check it. If an idea is still a build plan, call it a build plan.

Practical AI education should help someone make their next attempt better.

That's the kind of work I want this account to be useful for.
